questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the block dictates in direct carving
questions.learningObjective: state the constraints a single block imposes on a carver
questions.stem: A sculptor works a figure directly from a single block of stone, with no armature and no transferred model. What does the block decide for the sculptor?

options.text: The overall size and stance, since the figure can never exceed the stone and must stand within its footprint
The figure's interior, since a carver can hollow the block out to make the work lighter than the stone
options.misconception: believes a solid carving can be hollowed, which subtractive working cannot do

options.text: The surface finish, since a stone surface can only be polished and can never be cut a second time
options.misconception: assumes stone cannot be reworked, when carving and polishing are successive stages

options.text: The pose itself, since a figure without joints cannot be reposed once it has been cut free
options.misconception: attributes the pose to the material, when it follows from the block's dimensions

questions.explanation: Carving is subtractive, so a sculptor works only with what the stone already has, and the block therefore has a voice in the design. Its dimensions bound the figure, and its footprint has to hold the stance: a figure that overhangs its base is not a figure the stone will support, and a carver who wants an extended arm or a leaning weight has to find room for it in the mass that is there. The block also arrives with a grain and a bedding, so the orientation of the design is forced early rather than preferred. What the block does not do is decide the interior, which stays solid because there is no additive step that could clear it, or the finish, which is a later sequence of abrasives, or the pose, which becomes the sculptor's problem once the stone's limits are understood.
questions.hint: Ask what the sculptor can add to the stone, and what the stone will only let them take away.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Carving in the round against carving in relief
questions.learningObjective: distinguish sculpture in the round from relief
questions.stem: One carved figure is free on every side and can be walked around; another is cut back against the flat face of a slab. What distinguishes the two practices?

options.text: The presence of a backing plane, which in relief sets how far the figure may project and where it may be undercut
The hardness of the stone, since relief is only carved in soft material and the round only in hard
options.misconception: ties the two practices to stone type, when both are cut in the same materials

options.text: The size of the work, since relief is by definition smaller than any sculpture made in the round
options.misconception: assumes relief is always small, when scale is set by the function it serves

options.text: The place of display, since relief was only ever made outdoors and the round only for interiors
options.misconception: assigns a fixed location to each, which the two practices do not require

questions.explanation: The distinction is a single physical fact. A figure carved in the round has no attachment and is expected to be seen from any direction, so the carver treats every surface as a finished face and can undercut freely. A relief keeps a plane behind the figure, and that plane is a limit rather than a convenience: once the background is a fixed level, a projection that goes too far has nothing to attach to, and the depth of the undercut has to be read against the strength of the stone at that point. Relief is therefore not a lesser version of sculpture but a different set of conditions, and it is that condition which lets a shallow carving read as deeply as a free-standing one. Nothing about stone type, size or location follows from the distinction.
questions.hint: Ask what is behind the figure, and what that does to the parts that project.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Subtractive against additive sculpture
questions.learningObjective: classify sculpture methods as subtractive or additive
questions.stem: A subtractive sculptor removes material from a solid mass; an additive sculptor joins separate pieces together. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Cutting a figure from one block is subtractive, and building a figure from welded and pinned parts is additive
Cutting a figure from a block is additive, since material is being added to the form as it is carved
options.misconception: treats carving as accumulation, when the stone is only ever being taken away

options.text: Welding is subtractive, since the heat at the joint removes metal as the two parts fuse
options.misconception: describes welding as removal, which is a joining operation and not a cutting one

options.text: Both are subtractive, since every sculptural process has to remove material at some stage
options.misconception: makes subtractive a universal stage, which leaves the distinction with no content

questions.explanation: The division is about where the work starts. Subtractive work begins as a solid mass and reaches the form by taking material away, which is why the artist is committed early: the shape once removed cannot be put back, and a mistake in a block is a mistake in the stone. Carving in wood and stone sits here, and so does the roughing-out stage of a cast before it is chased. Additive work begins as separate pieces and reaches the form by joining, so it can grow, be revised, and combine materials that could not be carved together: welding, brazing, bolting, lashing, and the fitting of cast parts onto an armature. The two can be mixed in one object, and much sculpture is both, but a method is classified by the direction in which the material moves.
questions.hint: Ask whether the process begins with a solid mass or with separate parts.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the lost-wax process buys
questions.learningObjective: explain the naming and the capability of lost-wax casting
questions.stem: In lost-wax casting the object is modelled in wax, covered in a heat-resistant investment, and the wax is melted out in a furnace. Why is the wax called lost, and what does the process buy?

options.text: The wax is destroyed in the furnace, so each mould serves once and the cast can follow the model in any form
The wax is lost from the surface, so the bronze keeps every tool mark of the original modelling
options.misconception: believes the metal reproduces the wax's tool marks directly, ignoring the refiring

options.text: The wax is lost from the outside, so the investment shell survives and is reused for a second pour
options.misconception: claims the investment is reusable, when the furnace destroys it with the wax

options.text: The wax is lost in the finishing, so only the finest passages of the model reach the metal
options.misconception: places the loss in the polishing, where no wax remains to be lost

questions.explanation: The name is literal. The investment is a shell of a sand and binder mixture laid over the wax and dried hard, and when the whole assembly goes into the furnace the wax melts, runs out and burns, leaving a cavity in the shape of the object. The wax is therefore destroyed rather than recovered, and the shell has to be broken to get the casting out, so it cannot be used again. What the process buys is freedom of form. Because a flexible wax can be modelled over a core, undercut, and given deep recesses, and because every casting gets a fresh mould, the same design can be cast hollow, can vary slightly from pull to pull, and can be repeated in numbers. The metal arrives with the finish of the mould and is then chased by hand, so the marks of the modelling are translated rather than simply copied.
questions.hint: Ask what the furnace does to the wax, and therefore to the shell around it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould does to the object it copies
questions.learningObjective: state what fixing a form in a mould makes impossible
questions.stem: A plaster mould is taken from a finished clay model and is used to press copies of it. What does the mould do to the object it copies?

options.text: It fixes the form, so each copy is the same size and shape and the mould cannot follow any later change
It enlarges the form, so a small model can be pressed into a bronze many times its own size
options.misconception: believes a mould changes scale, which depends on the material and the press

options.text: It corrects the form, so flaws in the original are repaired in every copy as the mould is finished
options.misconception: assumes a mould improves on its model, which it records rather than edits

options.text: It flattens the form, so a three-dimensional model comes out of the mould as a relief
options.misconception: thinks pressing flattens a form, when the mould's own depth governs the copy

questions.explanation: A mould is a fixed record. It is made from one model at one moment, and once it has set it can only ever give back that model, so the first decision locks the size, the proportions and every detail into a reusable negative. That is exactly what makes a mould valuable, since it turns a unique object into a series, and exactly what limits it, because any change the artist later wants must be made by altering the mould rather than the model. A mould does not enlarge unless the material and the equipment are chosen to, and it certainly does not repair: a flaw in the model is faithfully repeated in every copy, which is why a cast inherits the model's quality rather than improving on it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a mould once it has been set, and what it is no longer able to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the firing of clay limits
questions.learningObjective: state the limits that firing imposes on terracotta
questions.stem: Terracotta figures are modelled in clay and then fired. What does the firing put out of reach for the sculptor?

options.text: Fine projecting detail, since a low-fired porous body is fragile and the clay has already shrunk around it
Any firing at all, since clay must be left to harden in open air rather than put into a kiln
options.misconception: claims clay cannot be fired, which is the definition of the material

options.text: Any correction, since a fired piece is a hard body that no longer admits the tool at all
options.misconception: believes a fired piece is untouchable, when tools can still reach fired clay

options.text: The addition of colour, since the heat destroys every pigment that is put onto the piece
options.misconception: assumes all pigment is destroyed, which is not a general rule about firing

questions.explanation: Two things happen at the kiln and both limit the design. The clay gives up its water and shrinks, and it does not shrink evenly: a thick leg loses proportionally less than a thin arm, so the thick parts crack as the difference opens inside them. And low-fired terracotta stays porous and comparatively soft, which is what makes it useful, since it is light and can be made in large sizes, but it also means that a thin projecting detail has little behind it and breaks easily. The sculptor therefore plans for a form read at a distance and handled firmly. Firing is a stage rather than a terminus, since fired clay can still be worked, and a sculptor who wants a hard surface knows to use a higher-fired stoneware instead of terracotta.
questions.hint: Ask what the clay does to itself as it loses water, and whether the loss is the same everywhere.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the grain of a stone constrains carving
questions.learningObjective: state how bedding governs the orientation of a carved figure
questions.stem: A block of stone is bedded, and the mason says it splits cleanly in one direction and resists the chisel in another. What does that govern?

options.text: The orientation of the figure, since cutting across the bedding risks the surface breaking away in slabs
The colour of the finished surface, since the grain is what decides which veining a stone will show
options.misconception: makes the grain a matter of appearance rather than of structural risk

options.text: The weight of the finished piece, since the bedding is where any hidden voids are gathered
options.misconception: confuses bedding planes with the cavities a stone of any kind may contain

options.text: The sharpness of the tools, since a bedded stone blunts an edge more quickly than a random one
options.misconception: claims bedding dulls the tools, which is a question of the stone's hardness

questions.explanation: Sedimentary stone remembers where it was laid down. It has planes of bedding, weaker than the stone between them, and along those planes it parts cleanly while across them it holds. A carver who works with that information chooses the orientation of the figure accordingly, sometimes turning a design on the block because the grain would otherwise run the wrong way through a projecting limb, and always knowing which direction a chisel stroke is likely to split. Ignoring the bedding is a real and expensive error: a large flat surface driven from the wrong side does not carve, it flakes away. The grain is not about colour, which comes from the mineral content, nor about voids, nor about the speed an edge loses its bite, which is a question of hardness.
questions.hint: Ask in which direction the stone is weaker than in the other, and what follows for a flat surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What bronze's alloying contributes
questions.learningObjective: state the working properties that bronze's alloying gives
questions.stem: Bronze is an alloy of copper with another metal rather than a pure metal. What does the alloying contribute to a cast sculpture?

options.text: A metal harder and less prone to corrosion than copper alone, so a thin cast can be durable and finely detailed
A metal that melts far below copper, so the furnace that casts it needs much less fuel than for copper
options.misconception: assumes a substantially lower melting point, which bronze does not have

options.text: A metal lighter than copper, so a figure of the same size weighs less than it would in copper
options.misconception: believes the alloy reduces weight, when the added metal is the heavier one

options.text: A metal that cannot be repaired, so a damaged bronze is past any possible restoration whatever
options.misconception: assumes an unworkable alloy, ignoring the long practice of bronze repair

questions.explanation: The addition of tin to copper is what makes bronze a material for sculpture rather than merely a metal that can be poured. Copper alone is soft and corrodes readily, and a hollow cast in it would be both fragile and green. Adding tin makes the alloy appreciably harder, so the metal takes a chased and polished surface, and it slows the corrosion that would otherwise eat a hollow form away. That combination is why bronze holds a thin projecting form and a fine chased line at the same time, and why it survives outdoors in a way that copper does not. The melting point is not usefully lower, the alloy is not lighter, and the material is readily repairable, which is why so many bronzes have been patched, re-chased and re-patinated over long lives.
questions.hint: Ask what changes in a metal when another metal is dissolved in it, and which change helps a hollow cast.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What produces the colour of a patina
questions.learningObjective: state the origin of a patina on a bronze surface
questions.stem: A bronze surface carries a green or dark film that is not the colour of the metal beneath it. What has produced that colour?

options.text: A surface layer formed as the metal reacts with the air and its impurities, so the colour records alloy and place
A coating of wax or pigment laid on by the workshop, so the colour is a finish applied to the metal
options.misconception: treats every surface colour as applied, ignoring the film the metal forms itself

options.text: The way the casting cooled, so each bronze takes its own colour as the metal sets in the mould
options.misconception: attributes the surface film to cooling, which affects the metal not its skin

options.text: A long burial in the ground, so the colour can only appear on a bronze that has been under the soil
options.misconception: restricts the reaction to burial, when it also forms indoors over time

questions.explanation: A patina is the metal's own slow reaction with its surroundings. The copper in the alloy oxidises and combines with the carbon dioxide and the contaminants in the air, and the products of that reaction form a thin adherent layer on the surface. Its colour therefore varies with the exact alloy and with where the object has lived: a piece in a dry interior browns and darkens, one in a damp place greens, and one lifted from burial keeps a stable excavated surface. That is why the colour of a patina is treated as evidence about an object rather than as a decorative finish, and why restorers hesitate to touch it. Applied wax and pigment do exist and do change a bronze's appearance, but they are a separate layer that can be removed without touching the metal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the coloured film is part of the metal's chemistry or something laid on top of it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The structural logic of a welded sculpture
questions.learningObjective: explain what a visible joint does in welded sculpture
questions.stem: A steel sculpture is built from rods and plates joined by an arc, and every junction carries a visible bead and a ripple. What does the maker's handling of the joints do?

options.text: It makes the structure legible, since the joint is where the loads pass and where the work is put together
It hides the assembly, since the aim is for the finished work to look carved out of one block
options.misconception: assumes the joints are always concealed, which they are not in welded work

options.text: It keeps the work light, since welding two thin parts is lighter than carving one solid mass
options.misconception: makes a joining operation serve a weight argument it was not chosen for

options.text: It substitutes for finish, since the pattern of the bead is treated as the finished surface
options.misconception: treats a welding artefact as a decorative end in itself

questions.explanation: A welded sculpture is an assembly, and an assembly has a logic that can be read. Each joint is the point at which one part hands its load to another, and the joint has to be made strong enough to carry it, which is the structural fact underneath the whole method. Because that is already the most interesting place in the object, the maker commonly leaves it visible: the bead and its ripple are the trace of the joining, and they let the viewer see how the work stands up. That is different from carving, where the form is a single mass and there is no joint to display. It is not an attempt to conceal the assembly, not a device for losing weight, and not a substitute for a finished surface, though a maker may of course choose a surface treatment of its own.
questions.hint: Ask what a joint has to do for the object to hold itself up, and what that makes it worth looking at.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Assemblage and the found object
questions.learningObjective: state what an assemblage brings into a new work
questions.stem: A sculptor fastens together a discarded chair, a rusted pipe, a torn sail and a shop sign, leaving each object recognisable. What is the method doing?

options.text: Building a new work out of existing things, so each object brings its own use and history with it
Copying the objects in a new material, so the originals serve as templates for a cast shape
options.misconception: reads the found objects as models to be cast rather than as the work itself

options.text: Restoring the objects to working order, so the finished work is a repair rather than a construction
options.misconception: treats a construction as a restoration, which puts the objects back in use

options.text: Sorting the objects by date, so the finished work argues about the order in which things were invented
options.misconception: assumes a chronological argument, which the arrangement need not make

questions.explanation: An assemblage uses existing objects as its material, and the reason to keep them recognisable is that their identity is doing the work. A chair carries sitting, a sail carries wind and labour, a shop sign carries trade and lettering, and a rusted pipe carries industry and time. Fasten them together and a set of unrelated uses meets in one arrangement, and the meeting is the subject. The decision is also a decision about where material comes from, since the objects are already made and the maker's labour goes into the relation among them rather than into their form. Nothing is copied or cast, nothing is repaired, and the arrangement carries no necessary date, though the objects' dates and origins are frequently part of what the viewer brings to it.
questions.hint: Ask what the chair and the sail already mean before they are fastened together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What makes a kinetic construction different in kind
questions.learningObjective: state what time contributes to a kinetic construction
questions.stem: A construction's balanced arms turn in the air, driven by a draught or by a visitor's movement, and it will not stay still. What does that change about the work?

options.text: Its form exists in time as well as in space, so part of the work is an event during the act of looking
Its material, since the metal used in such work is unusually flexible and therefore keeps moving
options.misconception: explains the movement by the metal, when the balance and pivot are what turn it

options.text: Its subject, since the movement stands for time itself rather than for any working mechanism
options.misconception: makes the movement a symbol, ignoring that it is a real and necessary mechanism

options.text: Its permanence, since a work that will not stand still is necessarily a temporary arrangement
options.misconception: infers impermanence from instability, which is a different kind of instability

questions.explanation: A kinetic work adds time to the list of things a sculpture is made of. Stone and metal are modelled in space, and a viewer can walk round them and see the whole form at once; a kinetic construction is only fully described at a series of moments, and the sequence of those moments is part of the work rather than a description of it. That is a real change in what the object asks of a viewer, since the viewer now has to wait, and often to move, and can never see the whole form held still. The mechanism is what makes it possible, and it is a genuine piece of engineering: arms balanced about a pivot, a low-friction bearing, and a source of energy in the draught or the visitor. The work is not temporary, and the movement is not a symbol standing in for a mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer can never do to a work that will not hold still.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a scale model can claim
questions.learningObjective: state what a scale model establishes and what it cannot
questions.stem: A model of a proposed monument is shown at a fraction of its intended size, with the figures in proportion and the whole mass captured in miniature. What does such a model claim?

options.text: The proportions and relationships of the finished work, which can be judged before any stone is quarried
The finished appearance, since a model shows exactly how the final surface will look
options.misconception: treats a model's surface as predictive, which a reduced model cannot be

options.text: The final cost, since a model is priced at the same rate as the work that it represents
options.misconception: connects a model to price, which is a matter of material and labour

options.text: The structural safety, since a model proves the finished work will stand without moving
options.misconception: claims a model certifies stability, which engineering calculation must do

questions.explanation: A model is a statement about relationships. Scale preserves proportion, so a model can show at a manageable size how a figure will look from the ground, how the tiers will stack, how the whole mass will sit against a building or a sky, and whether a committee will accept the arrangement, all of which are questions of proportion and sightline. It is valuable precisely because it is made before the expensive commitment, and it is adjustable in a way the finished work is not. What it cannot show is the surface, since a model's material is not the stone's, or the texture at arm's length, or the cost, or the engineering, all of which depend on the real material at the real scale. A model settles a composition; it does not certify the object.
questions.hint: Ask what a change of scale preserves, and what it necessarily changes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Installation and its dependence on site
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a work an installation rather than an object
questions.stem: A work exists as an arrangement of objects, light and sound in one particular building, and its components are numbered so that the arrangement can be rebuilt. What kind of work is it?

options.text: An installation, whose identity lies in the whole arrangement rather than in any one of its parts
A relief, whose components are fixed to a wall and cannot be moved away from it
options.misconception: confuses a built arrangement with a work attached to a wall face

options.text: A cast, since the numbered components are copies taken from one original work
options.misconception: assumes numbering implies a multiple, which here it merely records

options.text: A kinetic construction, since the arrangement changes as the visitor moves through the building
options.misconception: confuses the visitor's movement with a mechanism that moves by itself

questions.explanation: An installation's unit is the arrangement, not the object. Each component is in one sense an ordinary thing, and several may be unique works in their own right, but they do not constitute the work separately; the work is the set of relations among them, the room's dimensions, its light, its entry, its acoustics and its neighbours. That is why installation is dependent on site in a way sculpture is not: remove the arrangement to a different room and the work is a different work, or no work at all, since the proportions and the light have changed. Numbering the components is what makes reconstruction possible, and it records the parts rather than evidencing a multiple. A visitor walking through a room is not a mechanism turning.
questions.hint: Ask what would be left of the work if you kept one part and removed the arrangement around it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the siting of a monument decides
questions.learningObjective: state what a monument's location determines
questions.stem: A cast bronze figure is to be set up in a public square. What does the choice of position decide for the work?

options.text: The terms on which it is seen, since the square supplies an audience, a sightline and a set of neighbours
The date of the casting, since the position has to be settled before the metal is poured
options.misconception: makes siting a foundry decision, which it is not

options.text: The ownership of the work, since a work given to a square becomes the town's property
options.misconception: confuses a gift with a change of title, which is a separate question

options.text: The size of the work, since a square will only carry a figure of a stated size without crowding
options.misconception: assumes a fixed maximum scale, where the square is one constraint among several

questions.explanation: A monument in a public place is never seen as a free-standing object; it is seen from a distance, at an angle, in company. Siting decides all of that. Where the figure stands in relation to the approach determines whether it is read frontally as a portrait or in silhouette against the sky as the viewer turns, and a work that reads well from one point can be an unreadable profile from another. The buildings around it become part of its meaning, since a figure placed to face a façade is in conversation with that façade and one placed in the middle of an open space is not. The audience, the hour when the light is best, and the crowd that will gather there are all settled by the position. None of this fixes when the metal was poured, and none of it determines title or a maximum scale.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer meets first, and from where, on arriving in a square.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial argument of a memorial garden
questions.learningObjective: interpret a garden's layout as an argument
questions.stem: A garden laid out to commemorate the dead is entered along a straight walled axis and closed at the far end by a single stone. What is the layout arguing?

options.text: That the dead are to be approached in order and enclosed, so the visitor's walk carries the argument
That the land was laid out for farming, so the planting records a working estate of the period
options.misconception: reads a memorial layout as a record of agricultural use

options.text: That the dead lie in a fixed order of rank, so the axis sorts the graves by their occupants
options.misconception: reads a linear walk as a hierarchy, which the enclosed axis does not assert

options.text: That the ground is a public park, so the open space was meant for the town's recreation
options.misconception: assumes open space signals recreation, ignoring the enclosed approach

questions.explanation: A memorial garden makes its argument in plan. A single straight axis walls the visitor into a controlled approach, removes the distractions of the town, and delivers them to a termination that is chosen rather than found. The length of the walk is the time the visitor is given, and the walls are the claim that this is a separate place. Repeating an element along the way, a row of markers, a line of paving, a change of level, turns a path into a sequence in which each step is countable. What the layout does not do is sort the dead by rank, since a linear processional plan treats them alike, and it certainly is not agricultural or recreational, both of which would be a different kind of ground entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what a single straight walled path does to the visitor, and what the closing stone does at the end.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The narrative a war memorial selects
questions.learningObjective: state what a war memorial asserts by choosing a moment
questions.stem: A war memorial shows a group of soldiers in the moment of departure rather than in combat or in mourning. What is the sculptor doing?

options.text: Choosing one moment out of many, so the memorial argues for a particular account of what the war was
Recording the war as a whole, so the group stands in for every engagement that was fought
options.misconception: treats a single scene as a total record of a whole war

options.text: Documenting the faces, so that each soldier shown is a portrait of a particular named man
options.misconception: assumes every figure is an individual likeness, which the type usually denies

options.text: Filling the site, so the number of figures is set by the space rather than by the argument
options.misconception: explains the crowd by the available stone rather than by the design

questions.explanation: A war memorial is a historical claim in stone, and the claim is made by the moment chosen. Departure says that the men went out as volunteers and were young; combat says that they fought; mourning says that they are dead and the city is grieving. Each of these is defensible and each excludes the others, which is why the choice of subject is the sharpest decision a war memorial makes and why it is argued over long afterwards. A single scene cannot be a record of a whole war, and a figure in a group is usually a type rather than a portrait, since naming individuals would be a different and much longer undertaking. The number of figures may also be a practical matter of the site, but that is a constraint on the design, not the design itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the picture leaves out, and who is entitled to choose what is left out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit a cast sets on reproduction
questions.learningObjective: state what the casting process fixes and what it cannot vary
questions.stem: A bronze is cast in a foundry, and further castings of the same design are struck over the following years. What limit does the process set?

options.text: Every casting is very nearly the same, so the edition repeats one work and its variety comes from wear and surface
Every casting differs substantially, so no two are alike and each is unique in itself
options.misconception: claims variation so great that each casting is a separate work

options.text: A casting cannot be seen at all, since bronze is only legible in a photograph of the mould
options.misconception: denies that a cast is an object that can be looked at directly

options.text: Only one casting can exist, since the mould is destroyed by the first pour of metal
options.misconception: confuses a single-use mould with a single object, ignoring new moulds

questions.explanation: A cast inherits its form from a fixed mould, so a second casting of the same design is the same work again. What varies is small and consequential: the metal shrinks slightly differently, the surface takes the mould's texture a little differently, the chasing and polishing are done by hand each time, and the patina will go on developing at its own rate in whatever place it stands. Over decades that is a real difference, which is why a casting of fifty years ago is not simply a newer copy of one of last month. But the composition, the proportions and the modelled form are settled once and repeated, and that is the limit: the process multiplies a work rather than varying it, and a fresh mould is made for each new casting.
questions.hint: Ask what comes from the mould and what comes from the hand and the weather.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a photographic negative documents
questions.learningObjective: state what a negative records and what it does not
questions.stem: A photographic negative is examined under raking light and its transparent patches are read against a dark field. What does the negative document about a picture made from it?

options.text: The arrangement and the lighting of the scene, since each patch records where light reached the emulsion
The final tones of the print, since the negative carries the finished values in reversed form
options.misconception: claims the negative holds the print's tones, which it only makes possible

options.text: The number of prints taken from it, since each exposure leaves a trace on the negative itself
options.misconception: believes a negative records how often it was used, which it does not

options.text: The identity of the sitter, since the negative is the only record that can name them
options.misconception: gives a negative the capacity to name, which is the business of a caption

questions.explanation: A negative is a record of one exposure. Each patch of the emulsion was made by light arriving from a particular direction and at a particular strength, so what is on the negative is a map of the light that fell in front of the camera during that interval: where things stood, how they were lit, and how the shadows fell. The tone of any print is a decision taken later, made by the exposure time of the paper and by the grade of the printing stock, and the negative simply supplies the range. It says nothing about how many prints were made, since printing does not alter it, and it names nobody. Its evidentiary value is correspondingly narrow but real: it fixes an arrangement and a light, and it does so for one moment on one day.
questions.hint: Ask what physically reached each patch of the emulsion, and when the tone of a print is decided.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The direction of an intaglio image
questions.learningObjective: state how an intaglio print relates to its plate
questions.stem: A line is cut into a metal plate, ink is worked into the cut, and a damp sheet is pressed against the plate. In which direction does the image on the print read?

options.text: Reversed, because the sheet takes the impression from the far side of the incised line
The same way, because the ink passes from the plate to the sheet without crossing the line
options.misconception: believes the ink does not cross the incised line, which is the whole mechanism

options.text: Reversed in tone but not in outline, since a contour has no handedness to lose
options.misconception: thinks an outline has no direction, though a drawn hand cannot reverse invisibly

options.text: The same way, because a damp sheet stretches and mirrors the design as it dries
options.misconception: attributes the reversal to the paper, which stretches but does not mirror

questions.explanation: Intaglio is printing from a recessed surface. The line is cut into the metal, the ink is worked into that recess, the surface is wiped clean, and the sheet is pressed hard enough to force the paper down into the cut so that the ink transfers. The impression is taken from the far side of that cut, so the image on the sheet is a mirror of the image on the plate, and a hand written into the metal reads the wrong way round on the print. Every such print is therefore made from a plate that is reversed relative to the intended picture, which is a fact of construction and not a defect. The paper does stretch as it dries, but it does not mirror anything, and a contour plainly has a direction, which is exactly why the reversal is visible.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the line the paper is pressed against, and which side the ink is on.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: state what a relief cut gives to the printed line
questions.stem: In relief printing the design is cut away from the surface of a block, so that the untouched surface alone carries the ink. What kind of mark does that produce?

options.text: A line that thickens where the cut runs out and breaks where the tool has dragged across the grain
A line of even weight throughout, since a flat surface gives up the same ink at every point
options.misconception: assumes an even line, ignoring how the depth of a cut controls the mark

options.text: A soft line with no edges, since the ink spreads into the damp fibres as the sheet is pressed
options.misconception: describes an ink that spreads on contact, which is not how relief works

options.text: A line dark at the edges and pale in the middle, since the ink gathers where the cut is
options.misconception: puts the ink in the cut, which is the principle of intaglio and not relief

questions.explanation: In relief the ink sits on the surface and comes off it as a thin film, so what prints is the shape of the part that was not cut away. The character of the resulting line therefore comes from the tool. A gouge pushed in a curve gives a swelling and a tapering; a knife that meets the grain of the wood leaves a tear or skips; a shallow cut over a knot thins and breaks. Those variations are the vocabulary of woodcut and linocut, and they are a record of the cut rather than of a drawn intention. A flat surface does not give up an identical film everywhere, ink does not spread into the paper on contact, and the ink is on the raised surface rather than gathered in the cut.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the ink on a surface that is flat in one place and scooped in another.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The planographic principle of lithography
questions.learningObjective: explain why a lithographic drawing prints and the bare stone does not
questions.stem: A limestone is ground flat, a drawing is made on it with a greasy crayon, and ink is then rolled over the whole surface. Why does the drawing print and the bare stone not?

options.text: Because damp stone refuses the ink and crayon marks refuse it too, so only the undrawn stone prints
Because the marks are cut into the stone, so only the grooves can be charged with the ink
options.misconception: describes an incised plate, which is the principle of intaglio

options.text: Because the press drives the ink through the marks, so the depth of the mark decides the tone
options.misconception: makes tone a matter of pressure and depth, as relief and intaglio do

options.text: Because the drawing was made in printing ink, so the roller simply lifts what is already there
options.misconception: assumes the drawing is already inked, which defeats the process

questions.explanation: Lithography is a planographic process: the image and the non-image are on the same level, and the separation is chemical. The stone is dampened, and water is repelled by the grease in the crayon marks, so the drawn lines stay dry while the bare stone holds a film of water. Oil-based ink is then rolled over the surface, and it is accepted only by the greasy marks and rejected by the wet stone. The printed image is therefore the drawing itself, which is why a lithograph can carry the free and searching line of a chalk drawing in a way that a cut block or a bitten plate cannot. The image is not cut, not pushed through, and not already inked before the press is involved.
questions.hint: Ask what the roller is repelled by, and by what the stone has just been covered with.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The layer logic of screen printing
questions.learningObjective: explain how a screen-printed image is built up
questions.stem: A stencil is fixed to a mesh, ink is pushed through the open areas onto a sheet below, and the screen is re-registered for the next colour. How is the picture built?

options.text: One colour at a time through separate screens, so the image is the sum of its printed layers
All the colours at once through a single screen, so they mix together as the ink arrives
options.misconception: assumes a single pass can lay several colours, which stencils cannot do

options.text: From the far side of the sheet, so the layers are seen through the paper rather than upon it
options.misconception: puts the printing on the reverse, which is a separate printing arrangement

options.text: With each screen printing the areas the next screen will cover, so the order runs backwards
options.misconception: assumes the layers are laid in reverse, which they are not

questions.explanation: Screen printing separates the image by colour, one colour at a time. Each colour has its own stencil on its own mesh, the sheet is laid down and registered against the same marks, ink is pushed through, and the layer is allowed to dry before the next screen goes down. The printed picture is therefore an accumulation of flat layers, each contributing only the areas of that one colour, and the eye does the rest of the work by blending them. That is why the method suits flat bold areas and why it is the ordinary way to make a poster, and it is also why the layers are opaque and cover one another rather than mixing on the surface. Registration is what holds the layers in register, and nothing about the sequence runs backwards.
questions.hint: Ask how many stencils a three-colour picture needs, and what each of them prints.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal inversion on a photographic negative
questions.learningObjective: state why a negative's tones are the reverse of the scene's
questions.stem: A sheet of film that has been exposed and developed is examined: the sky is dark and the lit faces are clear. What does that mean for the tone of a print made from it?

options.text: The tones reverse again, so the print carries a light sky and dark faces, the way the scene looked
The tones stay as they are, so the print will show a dark sky and pale faces throughout
options.misconception: assumes a print copies the negative's tones, which reverses only once

options.text: The tones average out, so the print can have no more contrast than the exposure produced
options.misconception: supposes printing averages the tones, rather than exposing the paper in response

options.text: The tones come from the paper, since a developed negative records no tonal information at all
options.misconception: denies that a negative carries tone, which is the whole of its use

questions.explanation: The inversion is a fact about how the two steps work, and it happens twice, which is why a negative looks wrong and a print does not. Where light was strong, as in the sky, the silver salts in the emulsion are reduced to opaque black metal, so the negative is dark there. Where little light reached, as on a lit face in shadow, the film stays clear. Printing reverses it again: paper is exposed through the negative, the clear patch lets the light through and darkens the paper, and the dark patch blocks it and leaves the paper light. The print therefore carries the tones of the scene. Nothing averages out, since printing exposes rather than blends, and the negative is nothing but a tonal record.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the light is reversed between the scene and the finished print.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The mirrored surface of a daguerreotype
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a daguerreotype look the way it does
questions.stem: A daguerreotype shows a faint image in silver and dark tones, and when it is tilted to catch the light the image brightens and reads the wrong way round. What accounts for the look?

options.text: The image is formed on a silvered plate polished to a mirror, so the picture is also a reflecting surface
The image is a paper negative, so the reversal is inherited from the way the paper was printed
options.misconception: describes a paper process, where the image is on a metal plate

options.text: The plate is engraved, so the scene was cut into the metal line by line before the exposure
options.misconception: confuses the process with an engraved plate, which carries no exposure

options.text: The plate is covered with a coloured wax, so the image is seen against a dark tinted ground
options.misconception: supplies a wax ground, where the plate is bare polished silver

questions.explanation: A daguerreotype is a direct positive on a plate. The plate is silvered and polished to a mirror, exposed in the camera, and developed by vapour, which forms the image in the reflective surface itself, with the brightest parts of the scene standing as the brightest and most mirror-like. Two consequences follow from the same fact. The picture can only be seen properly at certain angles, because at others the surface simply reflects the room or the sky and the image disappears; the case or the box with its angled glass exists to control that. And the surface is a mirror, so the image is laterally reversed in the way a mirror image is, which is why a daguerreotype reads the wrong way round when it is viewed directly.
questions.hint: Ask what the surface carrying the image was polished to, and what a polished surface does to a viewer's own face.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the wet-plate tintype buys
questions.learningObjective: state what the tintype sequence makes possible
questions.stem: A tintype is made on a dark metal plate coated with a collodion emulsion, exposed while still wet, and developed while still wet. What does that sequence buy?

options.text: A short and cheap exposure, since a wet plate is far more sensitive than a made paper negative
A permanent negative, since the plate can be reprinted as often as a paper negative can be
options.misconception: treats the result as a negative, when it is itself a positive image

options.text: A colour image, since the collodion emulsion carries pigments of its own
options.misconception: credits the emulsion with colour, which it does not have

options.text: A transparent negative, since the plate is ground so that light can pass through it
options.misconception: supplies transparency, where the plate is opaque and dark

questions.explanation: The tintype exists because of a commercial problem. Preparing a paper negative took time and a return to a darkroom, which put portraits out of reach of a street studio working from a booth. A dark plate, coated with collodion and sensitised on the spot, is far more sensitive while it is still wet, so the exposure can be counted in seconds instead of minutes and the image developed immediately on the same plate. The result is a direct positive rather than a negative: cheap, quick, and each image unique. It cannot be reprinted, because the plate is the image, and it is opaque and dark, so nothing passes through it. Its colours are not its own; any tinting was applied afterwards as a varnish or a toned plate.
questions.hint: Ask what a wet plate can do that a plate dried in advance cannot, and what the finished object is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Tonal range in a gelatin silver print
questions.learningObjective: state what the gelatin coating gives a photographic print
questions.stem: A black-and-white print is made on paper coated with a gelatin layer holding light-sensitive silver salts. What does that coating give the finished print?

options.text: A wide continuous range of tones, since the density of reduced silver sets how dark each value prints
A permanent image, since the silver salts cannot be altered once the print has been fixed
options.misconception: confuses the permanence of a fixed image with the fixing step itself

options.text: A coloured image, since the gelatin layer holds dyes of its own above the silver
options.misconception: credits the coating with colour, which is not what it contributes

options.text: The negative's exact tones, since paper cannot change the values recorded on the film
options.misconception: makes the print a copy of the negative, ignoring what the printing exposure sets

questions.explanation: Silver salts in gelatin respond to light in proportion to the light they receive, so a patch of the coating exposed through a deep shadow is reduced to very little metal and prints as a light grey, while a patch exposed through a bright highlight is reduced heavily and prints nearly black. Every stage between the two is available, which is what produces a continuous range rather than a few separated steps, and that range is the reason the medium can hold a full set of tones in a single object. The image becomes permanent when the undeveloped silver is dissolved away in the fixer, not before, and there is no colour in the coating. The tone of a print is set by the printing exposure and the grade of the paper, not by the negative alone.
questions.hint: Ask what the amount of metal in one patch of the coating is doing to the value that prints.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Three-colour construction of a colour print
questions.learningObjective: explain how three monochrome prints are combined into colour
questions.stem: A colour photograph is made with three exposures, each through a different coloured filter onto its own negative, and three monochrome prints are then combined. What does the process build?

options.text: A three-colour image, since each print carries one filtered separation and the three together read as colour
A single tinted image, since the three prints are mixed into one surface with a dark pigment
options.misconception: makes the result a tint, where three separations are combined separately

options.text: A four-colour image, since the three filters and the paper between them add a fourth
options.misconception: invents a fourth colour from the paper, which is only the support

options.text: A brighter image than the eye saw, since each filter passes only the light of its own colour
options.misconception: assumes filtering adds brightness, when it discards most of the light

questions.explanation: The method is subtractive, and that is worth being precise about. Each exposure records the light that passed through one coloured filter, so the three negatives together divide the scene's light into three bands, and each monochrome print carries one of them as a set of densities. Laid together, and seen as one image, the eye recombines the three sets of densities and reads colour. The paper underneath contributes no fourth colour, and the result is not a tint, because a tint is a single even colour laid over one image. The combined print is also never brighter than the scene, since the filters have each thrown away the light they do not pass; the print is a set of losses that the eye puts back together.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three prints records, and what the eye does with the three of them together.

questions.topic: What a poster does to its message
questions.learningObjective: state the compression a poster imposes on its message
questions.stem: A poster carries one image, a short line of words and the name of an event, in type large enough to be read from across a street. What does it do to its message?

options.text: It reduces the message to what survives at a distance and a glance, discarding everything needing close reading
It repeats the message in several languages, so the event can be read by any passer-by
options.misconception: assumes a translation is included, which a single short line is not

options.text: It preserves the detail of a painted original, so the poster is a faithful reduction of it
options.misconception: makes a poster a faithful reduction, when the reduction is the point

options.text: It sets out the terms of admission, so the words carry what the image cannot
options.misconception: supposes a poster carries practical information rather than an invitation

questions.explanation: A poster is read at a distance, once, and often while moving. That sets a hard limit on how much can be in it, and every element is judged by whether it survives that condition: the image has to be one shape rather than a composition of many, the type has to be large enough to resolve, and the words have to be few. What is dropped is everything that rewards a second look. Nothing about the format requires translation, and nothing about it requires detail, since a faithful reduction of a painting would be unreadable at the distance it is meant to be seen from. The terms of admission belong on a separate notice, not on the sheet whose whole work is to make a passer-by look up.
questions.hint: Ask how long a passer-by has, and at what distance, and what that allows.

questions.topic: The audience of a broadside
questions.learningObjective: identify the readership a broadside is made for
questions.stem: A single sheet printed on one side in large type and given away or sold cheaply in a town carries a notice, a proclamation or an advertisement. Who is it made for?

options.text: The general public of that town, who will see it once, briefly, and are expected to act on it
A small circle of readers, who will keep the sheet and consult it repeatedly over years
options.misconception: assumes a reference document, where a single sheet is made to be acted on

options.text: A court or a guild, which will file the sheet among other documents of its own business
options.misconception: treats a public sheet as an internal record of an institution

options.text: Children learning to read, for whom the large type removes the difficulty of the text
options.misconception: explains the type size by a teaching aim, which the notices do not claim

questions.explanation: A broadside is a print for a town, and it is designed on the assumption that almost nobody will read it carefully. One side, large type, a strong division into blocks, and a message that can be taken in at a glance, because the sheet will be read standing up and then thrown away or pasted to a wall. What it carries is something that needs to be known and acted on now: a notice of a meeting, a proclamation, an official announcement, a thing for sale. The large type is a practical consequence of reading at a distance and in a hurry, not an educational intention. It is neither a document to be filed, which would be bound and small, nor a record consulted years later, which would be paginated and dated in full.
questions.hint: Ask how long a person in a street has for a sheet, and what happens to it afterwards.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Traces of lost-wax casting on a bronze
questions.learningObjective: identify lost-wax casting from the traces on the object
questions.stem: A bronze figure is examined and found to be hollow, with a fine seam running up one side, a small scar where a channel was cut off, and patches of differing colour inside the body. What process made it?

options.text: Lost-wax casting, since the wax was covered in investment, burnt out and replaced by metal through a channel
Carving from solid bronze, since the seams and scars are tool marks left by a chisel
options.misconception: reads mould marks as chisel work, though a solid block leaves no seam

options.text: Beating from a single sheet, since a hollow form can be raised from flat metal without any mould
options.misconception: assumes a raised form needs no mould, though such a method is a metal technique

options.text: Sand casting from a wooden pattern, since the channel is the gate through which the sand was poured
options.misconception: confuses a metal channel with a sand gate, which is not the same process

questions.explanation: The traces are the process. A hollow cast with a fine seam along one side is the two halves of an investment shell that met around the model; the small scar is where a pouring channel was separated from the casting once the metal had set; and the differing colour inside the body is the residue of the core that the wax was modelled over, plus the interior surface left rough because it was never chased. Together they describe a shell formed around a model, heated, emptied and filled. A solid block has no seam to show, a raised sheet is worked from outside and carries its own hammering rather than a parting line, and a sand gate is a feature of a quite different casting method. The evidence is not stylistic, which is why it is reliable.
questions.hint: Ask what a hollow cast with a parting line and a cut channel must have had around it.

Sculpture in the round, where the uncut mass is left as a mark of the working method

options.text: A cast, since the retained mass is the channel that carried the metal to the mould

options.text: An unfinished work, since the stone was never cleared away from the back of the head

It is not a sign of incompleteness, since a retained plane is a decision, and neither the plane nor the stone in it comes from any casting process.

questions.topic: Cracking in a fired clay figure
questions.learningObjective: read a firing crack as evidence of uneven shrinkage
questions.stem: A fired clay figure has a dull, porous, brick-coloured body, and fine cracks run through the legs where the clay is thickest, while the arms and head are intact. What does the condition show?

options.text: That the piece was fired to a porous body, and that the thick sections shrank more than the thin ones
That the piece was fired to a hard vitrified body, which shrinks unevenly and so cracks
options.misconception: calls a porous low-fired body vitrified, which is the opposite material

options.text: That the cracks were made after firing, since a fired body cannot crack at all
options.misconception: claims fired clay cannot crack, when cracking is a normal firing outcome

options.text: That the piece was cast in a mould, and the cracks are the parting seams of that mould
options.misconception: reads shrinkage cracks as mould seams, which run in a fixed line

questions.explanation: Two readings of the object agree here. A dull, porous, brick-coloured body is the signature of a low-fired terracotta rather than a hard vitrified stoneware, and porous bodies are exactly the ones that are light, workable and fragile. The pattern of the cracking then explains itself: clay loses water and shrinks as it dries, and a thick leg does not lose its inner water at the same rate as a thin arm, so the leg is still shrinking inside while the arm has stopped, and the difference opens as a crack. That is a fault of the firing, and sculptors who work in terracotta hollow thick limbs to avoid it. A parting seam would be a single line, not a network, and a body that is porous is not vitrified.
questions.hint: Ask how a thick section dries against a thin one, and what the resulting difference does inside the leg.

questions.topic: Joints left open in welded steel
questions.learningObjective: interpret open welding seams as structural evidence
questions.stem: A steel construction stands on two legs and is made from plates and rods whose joints are open and slightly rippled, with no smooth transition anywhere. What has the maker left visible?

options.text: Every joint where one part was welded to another, so how the thing stands up is part of the form
The seams of a casting, since the metal was poured into a mould and then freed from it
options.misconception: reads welding beads as casting seams, which come from a mould not an arc

options.text: The model in clay, since the structure is a translation of a finished figure in another material
options.misconception: supposes a clay original, which the visible joints do not require

options.text: The surface pitting, since the steel was left unprotected and the air has worked into it
options.misconception: confuses surface corrosion with the joining of parts

questions.explanation: The ripples are the record of an arc passing over the metal, and they run along the lines where one piece meets another. That makes them a joint rather than a texture, and since the maker has neither ground them down nor filled them, the assembly is what the eye reads first. It is also the honest reading of the structure: two legs carrying a load must transfer it into each other somewhere, and those transfers are the joints. A casting seam would be a line of a different character altogether, since a mould parts along a single plane, and neither corrosion nor a missing clay model accounts for a network of welds. The visibility is a choice, and it makes the load path legible.
questions.hint: Ask what the ripples mark, and where the load from two legs has to go.

options.text: So the turning counts the visitors, and each passage is recorded as another movement
options.misconception: turns a physical balance into a tally, which the mechanism does not do

The crates themselves, since the packing cases are the finished form the artist intends to show
options.misconception: confuses the packaging of a work with the work itself

options.text: A cast, since the numbered parts are copies taken from one original work in clay

questions.topic: A print and its plate set side by side
questions.learningObjective: use a print and plate pair to establish the direction of an intaglio
questions.stem: An etched print shows a room whose windows stand on the left. The plate is set beside it, and the same room on the plate has its windows on the right. What does the pair show?

options.text: That the print reverses the plate, since the sheet takes the impression from the far side of the line
That the print and the plate are two designs by two different makers working on the same subject
options.misconception: supposes two designs where the pair is one design and its transfer

options.text: That the print is a copy of another print, made by transferring the image off one sheet onto another
options.misconception: describes an offset transfer, which is not what the pair shows

options.text: That the plate was filed and re-cut, so the design was reversed after the first print was taken
options.misconception: invents a re-cut, where the reversal is present from the start

questions.explanation: The pair is the demonstration. Intaglio prints from a recess, and the paper is pressed down into the cut so that the ink transfers from the far side of the line, which means the sheet receives a mirror of whatever is on the metal. Windows on the right on the plate and on the left on the print is exactly that, and it is why an etcher works backwards or transfers a reversed cartoon. It is one design and one transfer, not two designs, and nothing about the pair suggests a print was copied from a print, which is a different process with a different set of traces. Nor does the plate need re-cutting: the reversal is a property of intaglio printing from the start, and the plate is displayed to show it, not to correct it.

questions.topic: Ink rolled across a drawn stone
questions.learningObjective: apply the planographic principle to a described print
questions.stem: A drawn stone is dampened, a film of ink is rolled over the whole surface, and damp paper is pressed onto it. The print shows the drawing's lines and nothing of the bare stone. Why?

options.text: Because the damp stone refuses the ink and the greasy marks refuse it too, so only the undrawn stone prints
Because the lines are cut into the stone and the grooves alone hold the ink against the roller
options.misconception: describes an incised plate, where the ink does sit in grooves

options.text: Because the press pushes the ink through the marks, so the depth of each mark decides the tone
options.misconception: makes the tone a matter of depth, which is not the planographic case

options.text: Because the drawing was made with printing ink, so the roller merely lifts what is already on the stone
options.misconception: assumes the drawing is already inked, which removes the process

questions.explanation: The described sequence is lithography, and the printing of the bare stone is the part that proves it. Damp stone and grease do not mix, so the water sits on the undrawn surface and the crayon marks stay dry, and an oil-based ink is then accepted by the dry, greasy lines and rejected by the wet stone. The roller passing over the whole plate without depositing ink on it is not a failure of the press but the point of the process: the image and the non-image share one level and are separated only by chemistry. Cutting the lines would be intaglio, pressing ink into them would be intaglio, and a drawing already made in ink would be a transfer rather than a print.
questions.hint: Ask what the stone is covered with, and what that does to the ink the roller lays down.

questions.topic: A foundry ledger read as a process record
questions.learningObjective: interpret a foundry record as evidence of method and of origin
questions.stem: A foundry ledger lists, for one casting: a wax model finished in spring, a plaster investment made, a furnace-book entry for a burn-out, a pour, and a line for freeing the casting from the investment. What does the record establish?

options.text: The sequence of the lost-wax process, and that this bronze was cast in a foundry rather than carved
That the bronze is a copy, since a ledger entry proves the work was struck more than once
options.misconception: infers multiplicity from the existence of a record, which one entry does not show

options.text: That the model itself survives, since a wax model that was recorded must still be held
options.misconception: assumes a recorded object is a surviving one, when the wax was destroyed

options.text: That the casting is unique, since one ledger line corresponds to exactly one finished object
options.misconception: conflates one recorded pour with a claim about the work's status

questions.explanation: Read as a sequence, the entries are the stages of lost-wax casting in order: a model, an investment built over it, a burn-out that destroyed the wax, a pour, and the breaking away of the shell. That establishes the method directly, and it is unusually good evidence because a foundry's books are administrative records kept for its own reasons rather than for posterity, so they are unlikely to be tidied afterwards. What the record does not do is settle the standing of the object. It does not say how many castings the mould served or the moulds made, so it neither proves a copy nor proves a unique object, and the wax model it records was burnt out, so the record is also the only surviving trace of it. That is a normal condition of the documents of casting and one reason the book matters.

questions.topic: What an accession register entry does and does not fix
questions.learningObjective: state the scope of what an accession entry establishes
questions.stem: A museum's register records: an object received by gift from a named donor, entered on a stated date, given an accession number, and carrying a value supplied by the donor. What does the entry establish?

options.text: That the museum has accepted the object into its collection under a number, and nothing about its worth
That the object is worth the sum stated, since an accession entry fixes a value for good
options.misconception: treats a donor's figure as a valuation, which it is not

options.text: That the object was made by the donor, since a gift carries the maker along with it
options.misconception: assumes a gift identifies a maker, which is a separate research question

options.text: That the object can no longer be disposed of, since an accessioned gift is permanent
options.misconception: assumes accession forecloses disposal, which is a matter of policy

It does not establish value. A figure entered from a donor is a statement of sentiment or of tax, written by someone with an interest in the figure, and the museum's own valuation is a separate professional exercise carried out on other terms. Nor does the entry settle the maker, the date, or the disposal question, all of which are research or policy matters. The register records the museum's decision, not everything about the object.

questions.topic: A condition report as a basis for a decision
questions.learningObjective: interpret a condition report as a decision document
questions.stem: A condition report on a terracotta records powdering at the surface, two old fills in the legs, a previously repaired break at the base, and an unchanging environment over the last twenty years. What does the report support?

options.text: A case for stabilising the surface and checking the old fills, with the long stability arguing against haste
A case for immediate structural repair, since powdering always means the object is about to fail
options.misconception: reads one symptom as imminent collapse, which the report does not show

options.text: A case for returning the object to its maker, since only the maker can restore a fired body
options.misconception: supplies a maker as a restorer, which is not who repairs a collection object

options.text: A case for re-firing the piece, since firing consolidates the surface of an already fired body
options.misconception: prescribes a second firing as a conservation, which it is not

questions.explanation: A condition report is a document for deciding, and this one sets out three things to look at and one thing that argues for patience. Powdering means the surface is losing cohesion and needs a consolidant, which is a routine and largely reversible treatment. The old fills and the previously repaired break are already interventions, so they are the parts of the object most likely to fail next and need checking rather than replacing. The twenty years of unchanging environment is the entry that governs the tempo: the object is not deteriorating quickly, so the treatment can be planned and the environment can be relied on to hold. Re-firing is not a conservation treatment and cannot be done to a fired object without destroying it, and the maker is not the person who restores a collection.

questions.learningObjective: interpret a studio inventory as a printmaking workflow
questions.stem: A studio inventory lists one plate carrying an early state of a portrait, two sheets pulled from it and marked as proofs, a second plate with a reworked proof, and a numbered edition of forty impressions. What does the inventory show?

options.text: A workflow of states and proofs, with the edition distinguished from both by its number and its plate
Three separate artworks, since each plate and each proof is a finished picture in its own right
options.misconception: makes a working process into three independent works

options.text: A plan to enlarge the edition, since the presence of proofs shows the number was not yet settled
options.misconception: reads working proofs as a promise of further impressions

options.text: A copy after another artist, since a second plate means the design was traced from a print
options.misconception: infers dependence on another maker from the existence of a second plate

questions.explanation: The inventory describes a working process, and each of its terms is a technical distinction. A state is one stage of a design on a plate that is still being reworked, so the first plate records an earlier decision. A proof is a proof, pulled to see how the plate is printing rather than as a thing to sell. The edition is a stated number of impressions pulled from one definite state of one plate, which is why the numbered forty are distinguished from the proofs and from the earlier state by both the number and the plate they came from. That is why a print is identified by plate, state and number rather than by the sheet alone. Nothing here is three finished pictures, and the presence of proofs says nothing about enlarging the edition or about copying anybody.
questions.hint: Ask what the three terms mean, and what has to be fixed before a sheet can be called an edition impression.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A carved-stone claim refuted by the object
questions.learningObjective: refute a material and method claim from physical evidence
questions.stem: A catalogue describes a figure as carved in a single block of pale stone. The object is hollow, weighs a fraction of a solid one of that size, and carries a fine vertical seam and a small scar where a channel was cut off. What does the evidence do to the description?

options.text: It refutes both the material and the method, since a hollow form with a seam and a channel scar was cast
It confirms the description, since a hollow cast in pale stone is a known and ancient technique
options.misconception: accepts a hollow cast as a carved block, which the mass does not permit

options.text: It shows only that the figure was repaired, since a seam can appear after any later intervention
options.misconception: explains a permanent structural feature as a repair, which it is not

options.text: It says nothing about the method, since weight and seams are not material evidence
options.misconception: excludes physical evidence from the question, which is the whole evidence here

questions.explanation: The three observations are independent and each of them excludes direct carving. A carving from a block is solid by definition, because subtractive working has no step that could hollow a mass, and this object is hollow and very light for its size. The fine vertical seam is the line where two halves of a mould met, and the small scar is where a pouring channel was separated after the metal had set. Both are the traces of a casting, and neither can be produced by a chisel. So the catalogue sentence is wrong about the method and about the material, and it has to be rewritten rather than re-argued: the description and the object cannot both stand. A seam is not a repair scar, and these are precisely the physical observations that material description rests on.
questions.hint: Ask whether a carving can be hollow, and what a parting line and a cut channel are evidence of.

questions.learningObjective: weigh a stated institutional purpose against recorded practice
questions.stem: A museum's founding statement says it exists to keep a permanent collection together and show it under stable conditions. What does the practice do to the statement?

options.text: It puts the statement in question, since collecting singly and displaying nowhere cuts against both halves
It confirms the statement, since buying at auction is the standard way of building a collection
options.misconception: accepts a usual method as evidence of the institution's stated purpose

options.text: It shows the statement is a matter of taste, since a closed gallery is still part of the museum
options.misconception: reduces a purpose statement to preference, ignoring that it makes a claim

options.text: It shows the collection is too small to display, since single acquisitions fill no rooms
options.misconception: turns a practice into a capacity problem, which the record does not state

questions.explanation: A purpose statement is a claim about what an institution does, so it can be tested against what it records doing. This one has two parts. Keeping a collection together is contradicted in a specific way: acquiring almost exclusively single works at auction, rather than groups or a body of related material, produces a set of individuals rather than a collection that hangs together. Showing the collection under stable conditions is contradicted more bluntly, because the gallery for a permanent display has been shut for eight of the last ten years, so a growing body of accessions is not being shown. The statement is therefore not disproved in law, but it no longer describes the practice, and an institution in that position has a choice to make and should make it explicitly. Buying at auction is unremarkable in itself; it is the pattern that is doing the work here.
questions.hint: Ask what each half of the statement asserts, and which recorded facts tell against each of them.
