questions.topic: What a mould fixes and what lost wax releases
questions.learningObjective: compare the constraint of a mould with the freedom of a fresh mould
questions.stem: A clay figure is to be copied in plaster, and then reworked in the artist's studio. First say what a mould does to the form, and then say what a fresh mould for each casting changes.

options.text: It fixes the form exactly, and a fresh mould each time lets the form vary from casting to casting
It enlarges the form slightly, and a fresh mould keeps that enlargement constant in every copy
options.misconception: makes a mould a scaling device, which it is not by itself

options.text: It corrects the model's flaws, and a fresh mould carries those corrections back into the clay
options.misconception: assumes a mould improves on a model, which it records

options.text: It flattens the model, and a fresh mould restores the depth that pressing took away
options.misconception: supposes pressing flattens a form, when depth is set in the mould

questions.explanation: The first answer is about the mould as a record: once it has set, it holds one model's size, proportions and every detail, and it can do nothing else, which is both what makes it useful and what limits it. The second is about the difference between a permanent mould and a destroyed one. A plaster or rubber mould taken from a finished clay model is reused, so every pull is the same object and any change must be made to the mould. A lost-wax mould is broken after one pour, so each casting is made from a new shell of a new wax, and the caster can vary the wax slightly, choose a different patina, or simply accept a hand-finished surface that no two pulls share. That is why an edition of castings repeats a work while a group of individually cast objects can vary within a design.

questions.stem: An edition of forty numbered impressions is published, with six further impressions left unnumbered. First say what the numbering defines, and then say what it leaves undetermined.

options.misconception: assumes a numbering rule fixes quality, which the numbering does not do

options.text: It defines the subject, since the numbered sheet is the version intended for exhibition
options.misconception: treats the numbered impression as the exhibition sheet

Nor does a number establish who made it, since a studio, a printer or a publisher can pull an edition, and it does not choose which sheet hangs in a show. questions.topic: Producing a patina and keeping it
questions.learningObjective: carry a patina's origin through to a conservation decision
questions.stem: A bronze's surface is covered in a green film, and a proposal is made to clean it back to bright metal. First say what has produced the colour, and then say why the proposal is refused.

options.text: The metal has reacted with its surroundings, and stripping the film would take the surface of the bronze with it
A wax has been applied over the metal, and stripping it would expose the shine that lies beneath
options.misconception: treats the colour as an applied wax, which can be removed without loss

options.text: The metal has been buried and recovered, and stripping it would return the bronze to its buried state
options.misconception: makes stripping a restoration of a buried surface, which is the opposite

options.text: The casting took the colour as it cooled, and stripping it would show the metal beneath as another alloy
options.misconception: puts the colour in the metal's interior, where the alloy is one body

questions.explanation: The first answer is chemical: the copper in the alloy has oxidised and reacted with the air, and the products form a thin adherent layer, which is why the colour varies with alloy and with the place the object has lived. The second follows from the thickness of that layer. A patina is measured in fractions of a millimetre, and the surface of a chased and polished bronze lies immediately beneath it, so an abrasive or a stripping compound that removes the green film removes the modelled and chased surface with it. There is no bright metal underneath waiting to be uncovered; there is the bronze, one millimetre closer to the middle. The colour is also evidence about the object, which is a second reason to keep it, and an applied wax could indeed be removed safely, which is the confusion this question is built on.
questions.hint: Ask how thick the reacting layer is compared with the chased surface beneath it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of the lost-wax casting process
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a lost-wax casting
questions.stem: A bronze is to be cast by the lost-wax process. Put these five stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Cast the metal into the empty mould, let it cool, and free the casting from the investment
Model the object in wax over a core, ready to be taken in a mould
Coat the wax in a heat-resistant investment and let it set hard
Burn the wax out of the investment in a furnace, leaving an empty mould
Break the investment away, finish the metal, and apply a patina

questions.explanation: Each stage is defined by what the previous one leaves behind. There must be a model before there is anything to mould, and the model is wax precisely because it can be modelled in detail and then destroyed. The investment is built over it and has to set hard enough to contain metal, and it has to be a shell rather than a solid block, which is why the wax is modelled over a core and the object comes out hollow. The burn-out then destroys the wax and leaves the cavity, and it must happen before any metal is present. The pour follows, the metal cools, and only then can the shell be broken, since breaking it earlier would destroy the cavity. Finishing the surface and applying a patina are the last stages and belong to the hand, not the foundry.
questions.hint: Ask what has to exist before each step, and which step destroys the material the whole process is named for.

options.text: Cut the details of the face, hands and drapery, working from the whole towards the particular
Set the figure out on the block, checking its dimensions, grain and bedding against the design
Take the block down to its rough mass, clearing the waste and defining the largest volumes
Finish the surface with abrasives, working the stone to the texture the piece is to have

questions.explanation: The order runs from the decisions that cannot be undone to the ones that can. The block has to be read before it is cut, because the size of the stone, the direction of its grain and the plane of its bedding decide the orientation of the figure, and a carver who discovers a bedded surface after cutting has lost material that cannot be put back. Roughing-out follows, and it is the stage that commits the large volumes, which is why the largest forms are settled while the stone is still thick enough to move. Detail comes third, working down from the general to the particular, and the surface is finished last with abrasives, since polish cannot be done under a rough surface and a too-early polish is wasted when the following cuts reopen the stone.
questions.hint: Ask which stage cannot be taken back, and which has to come after the surface is no longer worked.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of an intaglio print
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of pulling a print from an incised plate
questions.stem: A print is to be pulled from an incised metal plate. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Lay a damp sheet over the inked plate, pass it through the press, and lift the sheet away
Wipe the surface of the plate so that ink is left only inside the incised lines
Work the ink into the incised lines across the surface of the whole plate
Cut the design into the plate, working with a burin, a drypoint needle or a bitten ground

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each stage needs. The plate has to be cut first, because the recesses are the only places that can hold ink and everything after this depends on where they are. The ink is then worked into those recesses, and it has to be put on across the whole plate rather than dabbed in, since a plate is a repeating surface that has to be charged evenly. Only after inking is the surface wiped, and the wipe is the step that makes the process intelligible: it removes the ink from the level surface and leaves it in the cuts, which is why the print is a mirror of the plate. The sheet and the press come last, and the pressure is what forces the damp paper down into the recesses.
questions.hint: Ask which stage creates the only places ink can sit, and which stage takes ink away from the flat surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of a darkroom print
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of making a photographic print
questions.stem: A print is to be made from a film negative. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

options.text: Fix the image, wash the print, and dry it under weighted glass
Expose the sensitised paper through the negative under an enlarger for a judged time
Develop the latent image in a developer and then stop it in a stop bath
Place the sensitised paper under safelight in the darkroom and arrange the negative

questions.explanation: The sequence is short and each step is a condition for the next. The paper has to be handled under safelight, since it is already light-sensitive and daylight would print a picture of the window, so the loading comes first and the negative is set into the carrier in the same operation. Exposure follows, and its length is the decision that sets the tone of the print, since a second reverse happens here. The paper comes out of the enlarger carrying an image that is not yet visible, and the developer reduces the exposed silver to make it so; the stop bath halts that reduction, which is why it comes immediately after rather than whenever convenient. Fixing dissolves the unreduced salts so the image will not go on changing, and washing and drying come last.
questions.hint: Ask what light would do to the paper before you start, and what the stop bath is stopping.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a mould cannot carry to the copies
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what a mould transfers and what it loses
questions.stem: Explain what a mould does to scale and surface when it is used to make copies, and what of the original it cannot carry.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the mould as a negative. It is made from one object at one moment, and once it has set it holds that object's dimensions in reverse: every recess in the mould corresponds to a projection on the model and every projection to a recess, so what a copy inherits is the form, and the form includes the size. Scale is therefore whatever the equipment and the material make it, and a mould by itself neither enlarges nor reduces, though a caster can work at a chosen scale by the material and the press used. Then set out what the copy does inherit, and it is a substantial list: the proportions, the composition, the modelled detail, the incisions, and the surface texture as it stood on the day the mould was taken. This is precisely why moulding is a reproductive technique rather than a compositional one, and why a large workshop industry could turn one model into a great many objects whose likeness is a matter of arithmetic. Now set out what it cannot carry, and this is where the useful part begins. A mould records one view of one moment of the making. It cannot carry the effort: the time of carving or modelling, the knowledge of the material, the decisions taken and abandoned, the resistance that was overcome. It cannot carry scale as an experience either, because a copy is not the same size as a thing at that size, and it cannot carry the material, since plaster is not bronze and bronze is not stone, so the weight, the sound, the translucency and the response to light are all different. It cannot carry variation, because a fixed mould gives the same form every time, so a series of copies is a set of repetitions rather than a set of individuals; the things that do vary between copies, the ink on a print, the patina on a cast, the hand finishing the surface, are all added after the mould has done its work. The defensible conclusion is in between two errors. A mould does not merely transmit form, and a copy is not worthless because it repeats. But the interesting part of an object is not the form alone, and anyone who describes copies as though the mould had carried the whole making across is describing a category the process does not support.

questions.explanation: A full answer treats the mould as a negative that fixes dimensions, lists what is transferred, and then distinguishes the things that cannot be: effort, scale as experience, material, and variation. A weak response says only that a mould makes identical copies.
questions.hint: Ask what a mould records, at what moment, and what it has no way of carrying.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What actually defines a print edition
questions.learningObjective: explain how plate, state and number together define an edition
questions.stem: Explain why a print is identified by its plate, its state and its number rather than by the sheet alone, and say what an edition number does not settle.

answer.exemplar: Start from what a print has in common with a cast and what it does not. A cast repeats one form, and a print repeats one surface: the plate. That is the source of the image, and it is what makes the print a multiple rather than a unique object. But a plate is not static, because an intaglio plate is reworked. The artist bites or cuts further, scrapes a line, changes the aquatint, and pulls a proof to see the result, so the same plate carries several designs in succession. Each of those is a state, and a state is part of the identity of the impression: a sheet printed before the reworking and a sheet printed after it are not two impressions of one work, they are impressions of two works that happen to share a plate. Only with the plate and the state settled does the number do its work, and what the number does is set a limit. An edition is a stated number of impressions from one stated state, and stating the number is what turns a run of sheets into a describable set that can be counted, compared, and reasoned about. The full identification is therefore plate, state, number, and any publisher's or printer's mark, which is why catalogues record all of them. Then say what the number leaves open, and this is the part most often overstated. It does not rank the impressions: the ink on any one of them depends on how the plate was wiped, how hard the press was worked, the condition of the paper, and the state of the plate at the moment that particular sheet passed, so two impressions of the same state and the same number differ visibly. It does not establish authorship, since an edition may be pulled by a printer or a publisher from an artist's plate. It does not settle which impression is the intended or the best, which is a judgement about tone and paper made by somebody, not by the margin. And it does not make the sheet precious, which is a market question resting on supply, demand and the condition of the particular object. The practical consequence is worth stating. If you are cataloguing a print, the number alone is nearly useless; if you are reading a collection, the plate and state let you tell which of several designs you are looking at, and the number tells you whether the sheet belongs to a closed, described set or to the unnumbered proofs and artist's impressions that surround every working edition.

questions.explanation: A full answer names plate, state and number as three separate requirements, explains that a plate can be reworked, and lists what the number leaves open, above all the ranking of impressions. A weak response treats the number as a guarantee of quality or of authorship.
questions.hint: Ask what a plate can be changed into, and what varies between two impressions of the same state.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a daguerreotype's mirror surface does to the image
questions.learningObjective: explain the optical consequences of a mirrored image surface
questions.stem: Explain how the polished silver surface of a daguerreotype produces its appearance, and what that means for the object itself.

answer.exemplar: Begin with what the plate is. A daguerreotype is made on a sheet of silvered metal, polished to a mirror, exposed in the camera, and developed by vapour onto the polished surface. There is no paper negative and no separate print, so the image and the object are the same thing, and the surface that carries the image is also a mirror. Everything unusual about how a daguerreotype looks follows from that single fact. Take the angle first. A mirror reflects whatever is in front of it, so a daguerreotype held square to the eye shows the viewer the room, the window and the face of whoever is looking at it, and the image all but disappears. At other angles the reflectance falls and the image comes up. That is why a daguerreotype is almost never seen loose, why it is mounted in a case, in a small folder, or under a piece of glass set at an angle, and why a raking view of a plate shows the image best. The arrangement is not a frame for convenience; it is the only way of seeing the object at all. Take the reversal next, and it comes from the same fact. A mirror image is laterally reversed, so a daguerreotype reads the wrong way round when it is looked at directly. This is not an error in the process and not something that was later introduced: the plate records the light as it fell, and the surface that reflects it to the eye is a mirror. Consequences follow for the object and for the picture. The plate is unique, since the surface that carries the image is the surface of the thing, and it cannot be reprinted, so the image and the support are inseparable and any damage is damage to the picture. The range of tones is also constrained, being limited to the greys the silvered surface can return, which is why a daguerreotype reads as a fine-grained silver rather than as black. And the same surface that makes the image work also makes it fragile: a fingerprint, a scratch or a thumbprint is not on a copy of the image but on the image itself, and the tarnish that a resting plate develops begins to obscure the very reflectance the picture depends on. So the description to give is not of a photograph on a plate, but of a picture that is also a mirror, with all the viewing conditions and all the vulnerability that implies.

questions.explanation: A full answer derives the viewing angle, the reversal and the fragility from the fact that the image forms in a mirror-polished silver surface, and connects each to the case and the handling that follow. A weak response says only that a daguerreotype is shiny.
questions.hint: Ask what a polished mirror does when you look at it, and follow that through to the case and the handling.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why conservation treatment is judged on reversibility
questions.learningObjective: explain reversibility as the test that governs a treatment
questions.stem: Explain why a conservation treatment is judged on whether it can be undone, and work through a case in which a treatment helps and still fails the test.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the asymmetry that the principle rests on. A museum is not the last owner of an object; it is one of a long series, and it does not know what techniques will be available in fifty years or what a later conservator will know about the materials then in use. That is the whole of the argument, and it is a practical one rather than a moral one. If a treatment can be reversed, a later worker can undo it and try something else with better materials and better knowledge, and the object is no worse off for the attempt. If it cannot be reversed, the intervention is permanent, the information it destroys is destroyed, and the object can never again be treated on the original terms. Reversibility therefore sets the price of a decision: where the choice is between a reversible and an irreversible treatment with similar benefit, the reversible one should be chosen even if it is slightly less effective. Work through a case where a treatment is plainly useful and still fails. A terracotta has been excavated intact but with loose surface powder, and the simplest response is to consolidate it with a synthetic resin in solution, which penetrates, sets, and leaves the figure stable and handleable. Everything about that treatment works: the object survives handling, the powder is held, and nothing is visible. And it still fails the test, because the resin cannot be removed without solvent, the solvent will carry it out of the porous body along with anything else soluble that is in the body, and the consolidation is now part of the object rather than something done to it. Worse, the resin changes how the surface takes colour, so any later retouching or a later cleaning is working over an altered material whose behaviour nobody fully characterised in the field. Compare the alternatives, because that is what makes the principle concrete. Structural work on the object, mending a leg with a material that can be distinguished from the original and removed, is reversible. Fitting a mount that carries the load and can be altered is reversible. Reducing the handling of the object, or controlling the environment, is reversible and is usually free. The irreversible options are the ones that replace original material: re-cutting a break to make it join, casting a missing arm in a matching bronze, grinding a surface flat. Each of those may be defensible, and each has been done, but the decision has to be argued as permanent, recorded as permanent, and made by somebody who can say what is being given up. End on the practical test rather than the slogan. Ask what a later conservator can do with this object after the treatment, and if the honest answer is that the question will not arise, the treatment is irreversible and the burden of argument is on the person proposing it.

questions.explanation: A full answer grounds reversibility in the long chain of future custodians, applies the test to a treatment that works but cannot be undone, and contrasts it with reversible alternatives. A weak response treats reversibility as a preference for timid caution.
questions.hint: Ask who has to live with the decision afterwards, and what a later conservator can do with the object.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Converting a monument's scale into its model
questions.learningObjective: compute a model's height from a stated scale
questions.stem: A sculptor is making a model at a scale of one to twenty-four for a bronze that is to stand 2.4 metres high. What is the height of the model in centimetres?
questions.explanation: A scale of one to twenty-four means the model is one twenty-fourth of the full size, so the model's height is the full height divided by twenty-four. Put both in the same units first: 2.4 metres is 240 centimetres, and 240 divided by 24 is 10, so the model stands 10 centimetres high. The other route gives the same figure, since 10 centimetres times 24 is 240 centimetres, which is 2.4 metres. The units matter more than the arithmetic here, and it is worth knowing what the answer is for: a model of this size can be held, looked at from the ground, and adjusted, while a figure 100 centimetres high would be a study rather than a model and a figure 10 metres high would be unmanageable. Doubling the full height to 4.8 metres would require a model of 20 centimetres, at the same scale.
questions.hint: Convert the full height to centimetres, then divide it by the number the scale gives.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Working out the metal content of a bronze alloy
questions.learningObjective: compute a component mass from a stated mass fraction
questions.stem: A bronze casting weighs 20 kilograms. The alloy is 88 per cent copper and 12 per cent tin by mass. How many kilograms of tin does the casting contain?
questions.explanation: A mass fraction is found by multiplying the total by the fraction, so 20 kilograms times 12 divided by 100 is 2.4 kilograms of tin. The second route agrees: the copper is 88 per cent, which is 20 times 0.88, or 17.6 kilograms, and 17.6 plus 2.4 is 20, so the two components account for the whole casting and the arithmetic is consistent. The figure is worth more than the sum it makes. The tin is the component that hardens the copper and slows its corrosion, so a casting that has lost tin is a casting whose structure has changed, and an alloy described as 88 and 12 is a specific claim about a specific metal rather than a general statement about bronze. At 20 per cent tin the alloy would be twice as hard and much more difficult to chase, which is why the proportion is fixed by the work the alloy has to do.
questions.hint: Multiply the total mass by the mass fraction, and check by subtracting the other component.
